The composite WAM broadens absorption bandwidth to 112% covering 3.9–13.9 GHz.
Absorption rate exceeds 90% over both C and X bands.
The composite WAM consists of a traditional absorber layer and a dual-band FSS layer formed by a square ring and Jerusalem cross.
The FSS is printed on FR4 substrate with εr = 4.4 and loss tangent 0.025.
The absorber material (TP-15D) has dielectric constant εr = 20.3 and magnetic permeability μr = 3.55.
Replacing the metallic ground of a Vivaldi antenna with the composite WAM reduces RCS by up to 24 dB at 9.4 GHz.
Average RCS reduction of over 10 dB is achieved from 2 to 18 GHz.
RCS reduction is effective over incident angles from −80° to 80°, except for minority angles.
Radiation gain loss of the antenna with WAM ground is less than 1 dB compared to metallic ground.
The composite WAM thickness is 2.5 mm, thinner than some comparable absorbers.
The original absorber bandwidth was 66% before adding the FSS layer.
Surface current density and magnetic field intensity are enhanced at resonance frequencies due to the FSS.
The Vivaldi antenna used has dimensions La=60.5 mm, Wa=40 mm, substrate εr=2.65, thickness 1 mm.
Simulated and measured results show good agreement for RCS and radiation patterns.
The composite WAM maintains antenna impedance bandwidth from 2.3 to 15 GHz (measured).
The equivalent circuit model relates the FSS geometry to inductance and capacitance controlling resonance.
The composite WAM achieves better performance than recent works with 94.3%, 108%, and 77% bandwidths.
The RCS measurement setup uses six pairs of horn antennas to cover 2–18 GHz.
The composite WAM converts incident electromagnetic energy into heat, reducing reflected radar signals.
The study uses HFSS software for electromagnetic simulation and optimization.
